ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Support for scientific units in STACK.
ResponsesInList.Text: I'm going to beat the drum just a bit more on this spaces for implied multiplication issue a bit more.  Having a space between the number and the unit is the technically correct way to write a measurement.  Based on my student's inputs, it is also the way that most of them write units in the first place.  It seems enormously silly to me from a usability standpoint that we would insist that the *students* remove a space that is technically correct and that the vast majority of them use naturally. I don't really understand what the concern is about doing this.  There is validation display for students to check that what they wrote was interpreted correctly.  If the concern is that this opens up more ways for a student's response to be misinterpreted then doesn't that validation display solve this?  Also, if the space that is supposed to be there is the one between the number and the unit, doesn't that simplify the logic? If the standard Moodle question types (numerical, calculated) can handle this then why wouldn't STACK be able to?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Support for scientific units in STACK.
ResponsesInList.Text: Probably the primary reason why not is the complexity of building a context aware parser that would always know what the spaces mean especially if the spaces in front of the units should be handled differently than spaces elsewhere. The standard Moodle question types tend not to have to work with complex algebraic expressions and can therefore use a bit more sloppy string matching so the comparison to them is a bit unfair. Naturally, at some point in the future STACKs input validation and implied multiplication handling logic and parser might be rewritten and this kind of an feature (among others) could be added but what I see in the code side that would be a major overhaul and is not really something that could be solved in a clean way in the near future. So if I see this correctly you can get the units without the spaces or you can wait for couple of STACK versions until someone gets around rewriting that part of the parsers. Traditionally, STACK has not allowed spaces and if we were to add a special case for spaces in front of units it would break old things and that breaking would be done just so that students would not need to learn a simple rule: "for computers add the implied multiplication sign and for people typeset with a space". Just to make it clear, simply replacing a single space somewhere with a star is easy, but I would not want to build yet another kludge on top of the processing to handle that single case, especially as that simple kludge would break existing behaviour, the solution should be more general but the current form of the code base does not really allow that to be done. As a completetly different thing, if Chris happens to get interested is a maxima modification that would swap the multiplication operator that exists between the unit part of the expression and the coefficient part to an operator that would be rendered as "\," that should be easy to add but does absolutely nothing to help with this issue.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Support for scientific units in STACK.
ResponsesInList.Text: Joshua,I want to weep! There are a number of reasons why I've actively tried not to support spaces within expressions.  Use of spaces adds ambiguity and it adds inconsistency for student input (sometimes they are allowed spaces sometimes not....). Inconsistency upsets students (rightly) and opens us to claims for appeal in exam situations. One "meta-goal" of STACK was to try to nudge students and teachers into using notation in a slightly more consistent way and I'm failing to do this, because so many people ask for spaces as implied multiplication.  We know from research evidence that many students struggle with mathematical notation, and I think one reason for this is ambiguity (and also inconsistency, e.g. sin^2(x) vs sin^(-1)(x)....)  Babbage failed to convince people about using sin^2(x) as sin(sin(x)) so the inverse was consistent, and other comments about notation.  If he failed what hope have I? That said, I have added options to "insert *s" in some places, so I can't honestly say I've held on to this.  Currently the "insert stars" option has three values. 0 Don't insert stars 1 Insert stars for implied multiplication 2 Insert stars assuming single-character variable names In this branch ( https://github.com/maths/moodle-qtype_stack/tree/stack_3_5_spaces ) I've added three new options 3 Insert stars for spaces only 4 Insert stars for implied multiplication and for spaces 5 Insert stars assuming single-character variable names and for spaces One reason for not allowing spaces was to have a reasonably consistent interface.  It is now up to the teacher to provide this in their courses I suppose.... What do we want to do about things like 3 E 4 This used to be rejected, but now it will be valid as 3*E*4, interpreted as 12*E and so not the 30000.0 which is what the student probably intended. What about m g.  This used to be illegal, now it will be m*g.  Did the student mean mg?  How can we disambiguate. sin x will now be sin*x.  Then this is rejected with the following error message "You must apply sin to an argument. You seem to have sin*, which looks like you have tried to use sin as a variable name." I'm not adding an option for "space as function" or we will have total chaos! The coding wasn't hard to do this.  It has taken me 3 hours.  If STACK was a commercial project I'd just say yes and give the customer what they asked for.  But do we actually want it at all?!  Can't we send messages to students about the importance of saying multiplication when we mean it and only when we mean it? Will teachers understand all these options? I'll need some help testing this and identifying other patterns.  Help with maintaining this will be appreciated.  Existing users can, of course, ignore these new options. It is late. It is cold and raining. I want to weep!

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Support for scientific units in STACK.
ResponsesInList.Text: Chris, I'm sorry that I may be making this new suggestion a little too late to save you some work.  I've been pondering on this off and on all day.  I really appreciate the time and energy you're putting into this.  I'm certainly not trying to cause weeping.  I just can forsee this being a big complaint from us science types. I was giving a test today and while I was wandering around the room I was mulling this over in my head thinking about Matti's reply earlier.   I came up with several examples like you where spaces would cause problems.  What I've realized is that we don't really need "treat spaces as implied multiplication" everywhere.  That's a hammer. We really just want the implied multiplication in between units and numbers.  That would be more precisely targeted. So I have two possible thought processes which might work a little better. 1) Find the first instance of a unit in the student's answer and replace any spaces that is immediately before it with a *.  Don't do anything with other spaces. 2) Remove spaces and THEN insert stars in the normal places that you would. Option 2 will have some bad effects probably.  I took a look at the Input Tests and found several that would have effects that are less than desirable sin x a and b a or b But those were really all I noticed at first glance. Option 1 would probably still cause problems with something like "sin x g" assuming the student meant "sin(x)*g".  "a and b g" would be invalid anyways without parentheses "(a and b)*g" so that's probably ok. At the end of the day, if this is too complex to do well then I'm happy to admit its probably just better to leave it alone.  I'm not the STACK guru, just a chemistry teaching guru.  I know what's going to be most useful to me (and I hope some others) in the classroom and the most user friendly to students.  I don't presume to know how to code this. Although an early morning "well numerical and calculated can do this" on my part did not help... It was unnecessary. My apologies. So are these possible/easy/manageable?  Is there a better option to attack this?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Support for scientific units in STACK.
ResponsesInList.Text: And here comes the issue of context awareness: Is the question even using units is "s" an unit or some variable in a Laplace transform? Well this can be solved simply by remembering to tell the system that now we use units... So if the system has a defined static list of units it can find that first unit reference just fine, but what if you can add new units to the system from within the question? Then the parser itself has to be aware of the whole question and basically evaluate it fully to find those unit definitions before it can even parse stuff. So adding a targeting system to the hammer would also require building the whole command chain with fire control and intelligence gathering on top of it and the costs of that system would need to be paid even when it had no use. Oh and I want dynamically defined randomised fantasy units to make that system have to work even more to find out what are the units in the current context. But maybe that would be a bit too much, although teaching dimensional analysis with randomised units (as in the other students have different units defined differently) that have nothing to do with reality might come up. "a or b" is nothing when you could have 'sconcat(a, " bottles of beer on the wall...")'. Strings as an input may be mostly forbidden now but our friends on the CS-side sure would want them, but multiple parameter functions are a reality. The number of such small little details that could break something for someone is incredibly large and we surely cannot even imagine them all. That is the reason why I am very much against adding special cases that could limit the syntax to a general syntax.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Support for scientific units in STACK.
ResponsesInList.Text: Matti, Joshua, I've added some *trial* code because I want to try to better understand the issue.  Adding this code has been very helpful to me in that respect, but I'm not convinced it would be sensible to add it to the main branch for exactly the reasons Matti has pointed out. It is easy to ask for features and I want other people to use STACK: they will have other needs and wants.  I'll try to accommodate this. But we have to get them to work and maintain them!  This is especially difficult when we know (and strongly suspect) this is going to cause problems for students (in the long term) teachers (understanding an already complex system) and maintainers (unpaid, busy and not interested in using these features!) I like French restaurants because they only have one or two things on the menu.  They are delicious and freshly prepared, with care.  I'm very nervous about the British pub or Indian takeaway with more than 50 things.  Can any of them be fresh and nutritious? That all said, I'm very open to suggestions and will pursue them and I will support things I'm not going to use.  It isn't up to me to "dictate" how other people should teach....  I teach university students who are *very* bright.  They need to learn rigour:  "He that spareth his rod..." If I was teaching high school I would have a very different view. There is a balance in all this. If people really want spaces in expressions I've pushed a stub.  Please test it.  Let me know how you get on.... When it has been tested, broken, repaired (and I'll help!) I'll consider merging it into the main branch, but there is a limit to the energy I currently have for this. Chris

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Support for scientific units in STACK.
ResponsesInList.Text: I wanted to restate how pleased I am with how well STACK handles our approach to physics problems, it would appear that with a few small tweaks it would be ideal for physics! For our purposes, it would work nicely to have 8 different answer tests to choose from for Units and UnitsStrict. So as you suggested this would provide the following answer test options: Units/SigFigs, Units/NumAbsolute, Units/NumRelative, Units/DecimalPlaces, UnitsStrict/SigFigs, UnitsStrict/NumAbsolute, UnitsStrict/NumRelative, and UnitsStrict/DecimalPlaces. This flexibility would accommodate all conceivable scenarios encountered in physics problems. I have some reservations regarding installing STACK with the space-multiplication feature as this does take us back to a previous version of STACK. Moodle makes you perform a complete uninstall of a question type when going back to an earlier version and there may be some unintended consequences in doing so. The space feature is something that most physics people will want in that it allows students to enter a numerical value and unit in a familiar fashion. I believe it's hard for many, including myself, to get accustomed to entering 12*m/s or 12m/s, rather than the more familiar 12 m/s. Generally, physics people don't think in terms of multiplying the numerical value and corresponding unit, but rather think in terms of what the numerical value physically means by way of the unit. This is really the only situation in which I would want to use the space feature for multiplication. My suggestion would be to modify the code so that it would always look for a space (or two spaces to cover student typing errors) between a numerical value and unit for student input fields. Likewise, we would want to insert a space when displaying a numerical value and unit. Aside from this one situation, I see no need for a space-multiplication feature.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Ynt: Re: Webwork module uploaded to CVS
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi, The moodle-webwork bridge that Zbig uploaded 13 years ago worked only with moodle1.9x. There are new versions which have been created over the last few years which work with moodle 2.x and moodle3. There are basically two ways to connect webwork and moodle. The first and most stable method is to connect webwork as an assignment inside moodle. Students click on the "wwassignment" icon and are automatically signed in to a webwork site to do their homework. Their homework grades are then transferred back to the moodle gradebook. The install instructions for this option, which closely parallels the capabilities of Zbig's post are at https://github.com/openwebwork/wwassignment . It is also possible to connect webwork to moodle as a webwork question type which appears in a moodle quiz. In this method the student never sees the webwork site although the instructor will want access to the webwork site to prepare sets of homework questions. This is relatively new, still has some rough edges but it described at http://michaelgage.blogspot.com/2015/06/using-webwork-questions-in-moodle.html which shows how to install webwork questions within moodle quizzes (somewhat like STACK ). It contains links to earlier posts and to sites where you can view both the "question bridge" and the "assignment bridge" in action. The post also appears at https://moodle.org/mod/forum/discuss.php?d=315504

ResponsesInList.Title: Release of STACK 3.5
ResponsesInList.Text: It gives me great pleasure to announce the release of STACK 3.5. Thanks to all the colleagues who have contributed to this, including bug reports, suggestions, examples and code.  I do appreciate it. The code has been tagged and released through the normal Moodle plugin database . The release has some new features, mostly associated with enriching the input types. Added an export mechanism for single stack questions through a link on the "Question tests & deployed versions" page. Added support for optional Maxima packages through the config settings. Added support for multiple choice: the dropdown, radio and checkbox input types. Added basic support for scientific units, including a new input type and science answer tests. Any comments or suggestions, please let me know. Chris

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Release of STACK 3.5
ResponsesInList.Text: Thanks for posting. I do appreciate working on your own on a large project.  I try to discuss what we want, and might need, here to help people become involved and get a sense of shared endeavour. "Sometimes a decimal number in the feedback text is shown in scientific notation, and sometimes as floating-point numbers." At this moment I'm relying on maxima to display numbers.  The desktop version of maxima (shown in the screenshot) changes from decimals to scientific notation when you have 4 decimal places. Maxima has documentation on numbers and how they are represented here: http://maxima.sourceforge.net/docs/manual/maxima_5.html#SEC13 "The basic "float" type is stored in the underlying lisp's DOUBLE-FLOAT type which will almost certainly be IEEE 754 double precision floating point." Yes, we probably need additional functions which give us finer control over the display of numbers using scientific notation, or not.  Volunteers to write this?! First, it would be a great help if you, and others, could specify the problem with as many examples as possible of what you do and don't want. I already have a request for "Ephemeral forms for numbers." This is a form which operates at a syntactic level, to give us more control.   If you could help by developing the specification, then that would be a great start. Chris

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: I cannot draw geometric shapes with Latex
ResponsesInList.Text: I know that when you read those Using_Tex_Notation pages, it seems to imply they should all work right out of the box, as the saying goes. But in my experience, those things do not work by default, but must be setup on your system by modifying your LaTex preamble or your MathJax configuration so that they include the packages needed for drawing shapes and adding color. In fact some stuff, such as \line and \mbox, are blacklisted in Moodle, and to get them to work, you have to go and remove them from the  $tex_blacklist in yourmoodle\filter\tex\lib.php down around line 73 in most Moodle versions. These may or may not, work for you, especially the MathJax as I have it installed on my server with some additions. Here is my current LaTeX preamble: \usepackage[latin1]{inputenc} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{amsfonts} And here is what I have in my MathJax configuration: MathJax.Hub.Config({ config: ["MMLorHTML.js", "Safe.js"], jax: ["input/TeX","input/MathML","output/HTML- CSS ","output/NativeMML"], extensions: ["tex2jax.js","mml2jax.js","MathMenu.js","MathZoom.js"], TeX: { extensions: ["xypic.js","mhchem.js","color.js","AMSmath.js","AMSsymbols.js","noErrors.js","noUndefined.js"], }, menuSettings: { zoom: "Double-Click", mpContext: true, mpMouse: true }, errorSettings: { message: ["!"] }, skipStartupTypeset: true, messageStyle: "none" });

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: I cannot draw geometric shapes with Latex
ResponsesInList.Text: The Using TeX Notation document uses a lot of functionality that is present in the mimetex binary. This was originally the only way that TeX was rendered, but now works as a fall back. Currently, the included binary does not work on 64bit systems. A native binary or compatibility lib need to be installed and configured. If you want to use that functionality, make sure mimetex is working in TeX notation filter and turn off MathJax.

ResponsesInList.Text: Sam, I don't have experience with wiris, but I can give you some tips about getting TeX/LaTex to run. My examples are from my moodle installation, which is version 2.9.1+. The first thing we you need to do is make sure you have a TeX filter installed in your moodle. I prefer MathJax. In the Admin section, go to the filters section. I've turned on both the TeX notation and MathJax filters. (I can't remember why I've got the TeX filter turned on, probably for historical reasons.) Click on Settings to set up each filter. I have the TeX filter listed first. I pretty much use the defaults for the TeX filter (which is the first in my hierarchy). The only difference is that I have added one macro to my LaTeX preamble, which I use a lot. Likewise, in the MathJax setup, it looks like I'm using the default settings. With mhchem enabled, via either MathJax (recommended) or TexLive, you should be able to write the photsynthesis equation with `\(\ce{ 6CO2 + 6H2O + sunlight -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 }\)` which
apart from the `\(\ce{ ... }\)` is pretty intuitive, even without
the chemistry editor. In many cases, mchem deals with the chemical subscript (or
superscript) logic without explicitly forcing, say, 6CO_2. The chemistry editor may be more helpful for more complex constructs, ionic equations isotopes and the like. Note (from the screenshot below) that with mhchem the element symbols are rendered upright, rather than the italics displayed in TeX mathematics mode (compare with screenshots in previous posting). Chemists prefer this For photsynthesis, you could also use: `\(\ce{ 6CO2 + 6H2O ->[sunlight] C6H12O6 + 6O2 }\)` ; or `\(\ce{ 6CO2(g) + 6H2O(l) -> C6H12O6(s) + 6O2(g) \Delta{$H$}^{⦵}_{r} = +2803 kJ mol^{-1}}\)` Screenshot of the above three equations using the MathJax filter with mhchem configured.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Chemistry editor Atto plugin
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Colin "The MathJax filter is not working unless the TeX filter is on" Be aware that the MathJax filter and TeX filter are *different* ways of achieving the same ends i.e. the display of LaTeX-format expressions and formulae. When trouble-shooting, it's easier to work out what's going on by enabling one or the other, but not both. There should be no direct dependency between them. The TeX filter is the 'traditional' Moodle way of doing things using server-side installed/configured LaTeX binaries and related packages. These may be tricky to install and configure as up-to-date versions are not always readily available for different server operating systems. Also, the quality of the rendering may not be great, though is often improved by using PNG rather than GIF output format - or by using Daniel's new SVG output (in Moodle 2.8). The MathJax filter does a similar job but shifts the workload to the browser. Although, depending on connectivity factors etc, display may be slightly delayed, MathJax generally gives better quality rendering. Also, as you can just 'plug into' the MathJax Content Delivery Network (CDN) , it is typically easier to set-up and configure. In addition to the above, for chemical formulae display (as used by the Chemistry editor) you need the the mhchem extensions to be available to either the TeX-filter or the MathJax-filter. Again, installation of the mhchem binaries server-side may be tricky. In contrast, the mhchem is already part of recent MathJax releases, though you still need to enable it in the MathJax configuration The symptoms you describe seem to indicate MathJax is not working at all on the 'problematic' server. This suggests a problem in configuration, or in connectivity to the MathJax Content Delivery Network (CDN). Hence my suggestion to check the filter settings, MathJax URL , firewall configuration etc. In some circumstances other 3rd-party JavaScript/ AJAX libraries used in Moodle may also 'block' MathJax function. With the TeX-filter enabled, it appears basic rendering of LaTeX format is working, but the mhchem extension is not. Again, this could be an installation/availability issue on the server, or a misconfiguration. Be aware that if Moodle can't access the server-side binaries used by the TeX-filter, it does default to it's own MImeTeX package which does a  lower quality job of rendering LaTeX-format equations. As far as I am aware, MimeTeX does not include mchchem. So won't support the chemistry equation editor. Perhaps this is what is occurring for you. Hope that helps clarify things and is not just restating the blinking obvious. Others may have further/better diagnoses or suggestions. Geoff

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Chemistry editor Atto plugin
ResponsesInList.Text: Just a note that the Chemistry editor Atto plugin has been updated to version 2.8-1. Should work with Moodle 2.8.x or 2.7.x. This should have more consistent behaviour and work with either the MathJax filter or TeX filter including the new SVG rendering option in Moodle 2.8. In general, it also uses simpler, more natural, mhchem syntax and more robust separation of TeX mathematics symbols (now all wrapped in $.) After upgrade, you will also need to update the configuration e.g. by copying across from the default options in: Administration > Site administration > Plugins > Text editors > Atto HTML editor > Chemistry editor settings You can 'cherry-pick' or customise these to meet your particular requirements. Alternatively, complete uninstallation of the Atto Chemistry plugin followed by reinstallation of the new version will apply the new default configurations. In more detail: 1. The 'blank' buttons used as spacers in the periodic table layout can cause issues with SVG rendering of TeX in some browsers (particularly Chrome). As a workaround, a . (period, full-stop) is now used as a spacer. 2. The [arrows=pgf] or [arrows=pgf-filled] mhchem configuration options, if used, can also result in SVG rendering issues. So, a simple \usepackage{mhchem} added to the TeX configuration preamble is now recommended. This also give more consistent behaviour, comparing the TeX and MathJax filters. 3. Simpler, more natural, mhchem syntax is used for e.g. ions M+, subscripts X2Y3, bonds - = and 4. Up/down arrows now use ^ and v (with spaces each side) rather than (^) and (v) or \uparrow and \downarrow 5. Standard TeX mathematics symbols, greek symbols, italic characters etc are now wrapped by $ symbols to clearly differentiate from mhchem syntax and give more consitent editing behaviour. As a result, it is no longer necessary for the editor to add spaces around these. 6. The editor still adds a space before and after reaction and equilibrium arrows, for consistent display and editing behaviour. 7. There are new buttons to insert the TeX 'mid space' \:  and 'em space' \quad. Although mhchem usually provides automatic spacing, this may be useful if, say, additional spacing is required between a reaction equation and its associated enthalpy change etc. 8. Labels above and below arrows or other symbols (\overset, \underset) are now consistently displayed in chemistry (rather than mathematics) format i.e wrapped with \ce{...}. ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Jonathan As a follow up, I can reproduce your symptoms exactly with the MathJax filter OFF and the TeX filter ON (but without mhchem added to the TeX filter configuration). The broken image icons in your screenshots also indicate a TeX image rendering issue. So, you need to EITHER get the TeX filter working properly with the mhchem extension OR get the MathJax filter working with the mhchem extension. Usually, the latter is easier. So, I'll focus on that. If, for whatever reason, MathJax proves to be problematic, we can try 'PlanB', server-side TeX filter configuration. In Administration > Plugins > Filters > MathJaX check that the HTTP MathJax URL and HTTPS MathJax URL are correct. The defaults (in latest Moodle 2.7.x) of: http://cdn.mathjax.org/mathjax/2.3-latest/MathJax.js and https://cdn.mathjax.org/mathjax/2.3-latest/MathJax.js should be fine, but be aware that the MartJax CDN URL changed during 2014 and you may have the older, non-functional, address. Also, it may be that access to the MathJax CDNs is blocked by a proxy, firewall etc. In that case you may need to use the URL of  a local server installation of MathJax. If MathJax is working then the alpha symbol, or other simple TeX expression, should still render correctly with the TeX filter turned OFF (and the MathJax filter ON). You will probably notice better quality display by the MathJax filter as compared to the TeX filter. Then revisit Administration > Plugins > Filters > MathJaX and check that the mhchem.js extension is added to the MathJax configuration. My working configuration includes: TeX: { extensions: ["AMSmath.js","AMSsymbols.js","mhchem.js","noErrors.js","noUndefined.js"] }, Now mhchem syntax expressions (and the Atto chemistry editor) should work! Good luck! If you still have problems with MathJax e.g. with performance or conflict with other JavaScript libraries, then we can try 'PlanB'.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Chemistry editor Atto plugin

Something like: 
```text
<script type="text/x-mathjax-config">


  MathJax.Hub.Config({ 


    config: ["Accessible.js", "Safe.js"],


    TeX: {


        extensions: ["mhchem.js"]


    },


    errorSettings: { message: ["!"] },


    skipStartupTypeset: true,


    messageStyle: "none"


  });


</script>


<script type="text/javascript"


    src="https://cdn.mathjax.org/mathjax/latest/MathJax.js">


</script>
```

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: LaTeX not "properly" working
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello Justin, The TeX notation filter uses requires some binary executables to be able to run on the server . If there is a full install of LaTeX (usally TeXLive distribution) on the server, the filter will use this. This is normally configured to include amsmath, but the included packages can be changed with an administration settings. If full LaTeX is not installed on the server, then the filter will attempt to use a copy of a smaller program call mimeTeX. This does not include much of amstex and is not configurable. It also produces lower quality images. If this is the problem, you would need to install the LaTeX binary packages or you MathJaX to fix it. Which version of Moodle are you using? Daniel

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: STACK: Partial grading
ResponsesInList.Text: The score for each PRT is is initally computed out of 1. (That may later be mulitplied by other factors to get the total question score.) So, the score adjustment for each node to +0.1111111 (~ 1/9). Or, you could just have 9 separate PRTs.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: STACK: Partial grading

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: STACK: Partial grading
ResponsesInList.Text: Actually, STACK treats anything sufficiently close to 1 as 1.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Problems installing STACK on Ubuntu Server
ResponsesInList.Text:
Might be useful for someone, we managed to make default version of Maxima in Debian Jessie (Maxima 5.34.1 and GCL 2.6.12) work without any issues, thus no need to compile anything or backport. You need optimised version of maxima bundle created using documentation , then it works smooth and there are no errors in health-check. Step-by step guide for you, courtesy of Lancaster University CIS: 1. In Moodle STACK configuration set "Platform type" to "Linux" (not optimised) and "Maxima command" to empty value. Run the health-check script. It may contain errors which could be ignored, scroll to "Debug info" > " Context use", it should contain something similar to: 
```text
Platform: unix-optimised
Maxima shell command: maxima
Maxima initial command: load("/srv/data/moodle/stack/maximalocal.mac");


Maxima timeout: 10
```
 The Maxima initial command above is the one we need to produce optimised version. 2. Login to one of the web-servers, become root. Check what maxima version we have and what the LISP implementation is in use: 
```text
root@moodle:~# maxima --list-avail
Available versions:
version 5.34.1, lisp gcl
```
 gcl is the default implementation in Debian, and we will use it. Thus, the portion of maxima optimising documentation we need is GCL . 3. Run maxima and load /srv/data/moodle/stack/maximalocal.mac using command in step 1 above: 
```text
root@moodle:~# maxima
Maxima 5.34.1 
http://maxima.sourceforge.net

using Lisp GNU Common Lisp (GCL) GCL 2.6.12 (a.k.a. GCL)
Distributed under the GNU Public License. See the file COPYING.
Dedicated to the memory of William Schelter.
The function bug_report() provides bug reporting information.
(%i1) load("/srv/data/moodle/stack/maximalocal.mac");
```

```text
[ STACK-Maxima started, library version 2015090900 ]

```
 If you have already run the load command before and graphical libraries ( /usr/share/maxima/5.34.1/share/draw/grcommon.lisp ) have been compiled already, the output might be shorter: 
```text
(%i1) load("/srv/data/moodle/stack/maximalocal.mac");

Loading /root/.maxima/binary/binary-gcl/share/draw/grcommon.o
start address -T 0x25e0ee0 Finished loading /root/.maxima/binary/binary-gcl/share/draw/grcommon.o
Loading /root/.maxima/binary/binary-gcl/share/draw/gnuplot.o

```
 Notice, that compiling /usr/share/maxima/5.34.1/share/draw/grcommon.lisp require gcc to be installed in the system. 4. Without leaving maxima console, same optimised binary in Moodle data directory: 
```text
(%i1) :lisp (si::save-system "/srv/data/moodle/stack/maxima-optimised")
```
 5. Now it is time to reconfigure Moodle. In Moodle STACK configuration set "Platform type" to " Linux (optimised) ". Set "Maxima command" to: 
```text
timeout --kill-after=10s 10s /srv/data/moodle/stack/maxima-optimised -eval '(cl-user::run)'
```
 The above format will make sure that command is never run for more than 10 seconds, thus will not cause performance issues. Save the configuration. Now run the health-check script, scroll down and press "Clear the cache". The loaded health check result should contain no errors. If you see some broken formula images, but health-check does not report errors, this has nothing to do with maxima or STACK, check TeX Notation filter settings, you most likely do not have texlive package installed on your system. ResponsesInList.Title: Modest multiple choice input types for STACK.
ResponsesInList.Text: There has been some discussion on another thread about a new "scientific units" input type for STACK . In parallel to these developments I have been working on *modest* multiple choice support for STACK.  STACK version 2 had MCQ question inputs, but since I hardly ever need them and rather ran out of steam, they never made it back into the code for STACK 3.0. Until now. I have pushed combined code for units and MCQ into this branch: https://github.com/maths/moodle-qtype_stack/tree/stack_3_5 This code is ready for testing and comments.   Please note the design decisions and compromises I have documented here: https://github.com/maths/moodle-qtype_stack/blob/stack_3_5/doc/en/Authoring/MCQ.md If this code is useful, used, and people are willing to help I may add more features in the future. The plan is to release a new version of STACK as STACK 3.5 at the end of January 2016 containing the MCQ and units inputs. I would really appreciate help with testing and documentation before then. I would particularly value people sending me some sample questions, and  will add these to STACK's "demo course" and authoring notes.  This is probably the easiest way other people can help start to contribute to STACK development. Please don't be shy! Some specific questions which need to be resolved before the code is released: How important is "shuffle" and can one of the more advanced Moodle developers suggest a mechanism? Currently dropdown (select), radio and checkbox types return a Maxima list.  My original thought was to have consistency across all input types, and since checkbox needs lists, the others return a list with a single element.  This looks strange on student validation.  I'm beginning to think I should re-factor dropdown and radio to return an expression, not a list of one expression.  Any comments? Chris

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Problem with function ode2 in STACK
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Chris just because I asked a similar question recently: We tell the that \(\int \frac{dx}{x} = \ln (x) + c\) for \(x>0\) . When they need it for \(x<0\) , we ask them to substitute with \(y=-x\) . (Or as appropriate if it's a more complicated integral with several poles at different places.) If we tell them that \(\int \frac{dx}{x} = \ln |x| + c\) , they tend to think that \(\int_{-1}^1 \frac{dx}{x} = \ln|1| - \ln|-1| = 0\) . ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Using plot2d command in STACK system
ResponsesInList.Text: STACK only allows users (teachers or students) to use *some* of the Maxima commands, but not all of them,  plot2d is a Maxima command which is not supported in STACK.  To create plots in STACK you need to use the "plot" command, which is a safer wrapper for plot2d.  Note that plot2d writes files to the server , so we have to restrict what people can do with it! Documentation for the master branch of the code is on https://github.com/maths/moodle-qtype_stack/blob/master/doc/en/CAS/Plots.md with examples, but you should check the local documentation on your server to see which options you have available.  There have been some recent changes. In the case of your example, x^2+y^2 is an expression with two variables.  In Maxima, plot2d(x^2+y^2, [x, -1, 1], [y, -1, 1]) does not work either.  You need to create a single variable expression, to use plot2d (or plot in STACK). It is often worth using the desktop version of Maxima to check if your code works outside STACK. Chris

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Using MathType with Moodle
ResponsesInList.Text: Joelle, you're correct that the "MathType information" shouldn't be included with the translation. I have edited the article with the instruction to make sure these two boxes are unchecked ("Include translator name in translation" and "Include MathType data in translation"). Other than that, I don't know what might have gone wrong. Following these instructions will produce the best results: In MathType, choose the "TeX -- LaTeX 2.09 and later" translator. In MathType's Format menu, make sure Inline Equation is not checked. That should produce code that begins with a backslash and an open bracket, and ends with a backslash and a close bracket: \[{x^2} - 4x - 12 = 0\] The double dollar signs are OK, as far as Moodle is concerned, but it's better to use the backslash-bracket delimiters. The single dollar sign will not work with the built-in TeX filter, but will work with some other filters -- ASCIIMathML.js being one.

ResponsesInList.Title: Chemistry Equilibrium Expressions
ResponsesInList.Text: A fairly run of the mill chemistry problem might be: Give the equilibrium expression, K c for the reaction HF(aq) ⇌ H + (aq) + F - (aq). The answer would be: \( K_{c} = \frac {[H^{+}][F^{-}]}{[HF]} \) The symbols here are pretty specific in that \( [H^{+}] \) means the molarity of the H + ion.  Is this something that I can check using STACK ?  I'm assuming that there is a way to do it, but I'm concerned that the charges on those ions and the necessary structure is going to cause problems... Any suggestions on how to make this work?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Chemistry Equilibrium Expressions
ResponsesInList.Text: Joshua, This is a question I got asked a lot when I developed the dragmath equation editor!  I.e. can we use it to enter chemistry formulae?!  I'm very sorry, but STACK is designed to assess mathematical expressions.  The notation for expressions used in Chemistry, such as [H^+] won't be parsed by STACK. What is needed is a "chemistry input type" which will parse chemistry expressions and express them in a way which Maxima will be happy with. This would be a valuable addition to STACK.  I'm not in a position to develop this, but I will help someone else.  I taught maths for chemical engineers a couple of years ago and became painfully aware that I'd forgotten most my A-level (school) chemistry! Developing a new input type is not that difficult.  In particular, it is probably one of the ways to extend STACK which is least disruptive to the rest of the code and which relies on knowing very little about the rest of the code base. Examples are in https://github.com/maths/moodle-qtype_stack/tree/master/stack/input I'd start with the text area (algebraic equivalence is too close to the default values) and write a "chemistry parser" in PHP.  )BUT anyone thinking of this, please contact me first and I'll help you!) We would also need a library to display chemical formulae, written in Maxima, which outputs in LaTeX.  This is the easy bit. If someone would like to initiate a project in this area I will certainly help, but my current focus for STACK over the next few months is getting the "reasoning by equivalence" input type ( https://github.com/maths/moodle-qtype_stack/tree/equiv_input ) into a sate which students can use in anger. Chris

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Chemistry Equilibrium Expressions
ResponsesInList.Text: I have 'wrestled' with chemistry notation in Moodle for some time. Indeed, I was one of the folks who asked Chris about possible chemistry support from the DragMath (Java applet TeX/MathML editor) plugin, some years ago. The use of the mhchem extension to TeX/LaTeX, which can be added to Moodle via the configuration of the TeX filter and/or the MathJax filter (probably easiest) should help with the construction of chemical equations but probably not with the automated assessment. Similarly, the Atto Chemistry plugin (mentioned by Colin), which uses mhchem, may be more convenient for building chemical equations and expressions. However, like most GUI editors, it does not produce the most parsimonious code (think FrontPage or DreamWeaver with HTML!). Part of the complexity is that your equilibrium expression example mixes maths and chemistry which have different display conventions. For example, in maths text characters typically represent variables and are displayed in italics whereas in chemistry text characters are typically element symbols and are displayed upright. So, if this kind-of-thing bothers you, the example of: ```text \( K_c=\frac{[H^{+}][F^{-}]}{[HF]} \) ``` \( K_c=\frac{[H^{+}][F^{-}]}{[HF]} \) should probably be (using default TeX/MathJax filter, as in this forum) ```text \( K_\mathrm{c}=\frac{[\mathrm{H^{+}}][\mathrm{F^{-}}]}{[\mathrm{HF}]} \) ``` \( K_\mathrm{c}=\frac{[\mathrm{H^{+}}][\mathrm{F^{-}}]}{[\mathrm{HF}]} \) With the mhchem extension to TeX/MathJax, this would be the somewhat simpler: ```text \( K_\ce{c}=\frac{[\ce{H^+}][\ce{F^-}]}{[\ce{HF}]} \) ``` \( K_\mathrm{c}=\frac{[\mathrm{H^{+}}][\mathrm{F^{-}}]}{[\mathrm{HF}]} \) Actually, in mhchem syntax, \ce{H^+} could be further simplified to just \ce{H+}. The ^ is only required, for example, in \ce{SO4^2-} Using the Atto Chemistry Editor plugin, a few button-clicks from the 'Symbols and units tab' could give you: ```text \(\ce{ ${K}_\ce{c} $$=$$ \frac{[\ce{A}][\ce{B}]}{[\ce{C}]}$ }\) ``` \( K_\mathrm{c}=\frac{[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]}{[\mathrm{C}]} \) which could then be keyboard-edited to give the required: ```text \(\ce{ ${K}_\ce{c} $$=$$ \frac{[\ce{H+}][\ce{F-}]}{[\ce{HF}]}$ }\) ``` \( K_\mathrm{c}=\frac{[\mathrm{H^{+}}][\mathrm{F^{-}}]}{[\mathrm{HF}]} \) So, given all the above and other possible variations, it will be tricky to build any sort of system for automated assessment of 'freeform' TeX/mhchem answers. So, it may be worth considering other Moodle Quiz question types, such a multiple-choice or perhaps drag-and-drop gap-filling (e.g. where the learner is asked to build equilibrium expressions from existing building-blocks). The existing chemistry tools should, at least, help with the construction of such questions. https://www.ctan.org/pkg/mhchem http://www.ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/mhchem/mhchem.pdf https://moodle.org/plugins/stats.php?plugin=atto_chemistry

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Chemistry Equilibrium Expressions
ResponsesInList.Text:
I have thought more than a bit about using some of the drag and drop question types to accomplish this, but it becomes pretty difficult to actually pull that off.  None of the OU Drag and Drop types allow for transposition of elements that would really be required because \( K_c=\frac{[H^{+}][F^{-}]}{[HF]} \) and \( K_c=\frac{[F^{-}][H^{+}]}{[HF]} \) are really no different.  Also, an example like mine where there are different numbers of substances in the numerator and denominator would be dead giveaways as to the structure since the drag and drop types would show a box for you to drag an element into. If this were for a summative test, I'd have no problem with using multiple choice.  Instead I'm using this in a practice assignment.  (I actually still do all my tests in class on paper.)  But multiple choice early on in the learning process gives people familiar with the content a chance even if they don't know the information cold yet.  That breeds overconfidence and I try to avoid that if possible. In my head, I was hoping for something like a variable group.  So define the following: \( A = [H^{+}] \\
B = [F^{-}] \\
C = [HF] \) Then have something that might run to parse the student input to simplify \( K_c=\frac{[H^{+}][F^{-}]}{[HF]} \) down to \( K_c=\frac{AB}{C} \) and then run the algebraic equivalence test.  This idea might be useful other places also.  I'm guessing something like this is basically what Chris was talking about before in terms of an input type.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Chemistry Equilibrium Expressions
ResponsesInList.Text: The easiest approach might be to have the students make this substitution themselves.  Give them a set of variables to represent all of the possible molarities in the problem statement, and then have the enter the algebraic expression into STACK for evaluation. Whether this will work depends on the level of your students mathematically in understanding variable substitution. If they can do this, it has the advantage of reinforcing this skill for them. If they are learning beginning algebra along with the chemistry class that may not work. I did some work embedding my Mathslate into questions editor using a customizable filter, but never found a reason to bring it to production.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Chemistry Equilibrium Expressions
ResponsesInList.Text: Yes, Daniel's MathSlate may be a good option. it is easily customisable, has a nice drag-and-drop interface, and emphasises the logic/structure of an expression. See https://moodle.org/mod/forum/discuss.php?d=283205 A while back, I did experiment with a ChemSlate version of MathSlate that supported the mhchem extension to TeX/MathJax. However, I was focusing on basic (reaction) chemical equations and got 'bogged-down' in the technical details of  the conversion of MathML, MathJax snippets, TeX-mhchem syntax etc. So, my attention switched to a simpler (to my mind!) system based on the Atto Equation editor, instead. In the context of equilibrium expressions, MathSlate may well be a better fit. Perhaps an EquilibriumSlate?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Chemistry Equilibrium Expressions
ResponsesInList.Text: Agree with your pedagogic points about different assessment methods and can see that existing drag-and-drop question types may not quite fit-the-bill. Still think there may be some formative 'mileage' in a custom Equilibrium drag-and-drop Question type similar to those by Carl LeBlond for Organic Chemistry Nomenclature or Newman Projections . Of course, will need careful design and logic to avoid being trivially simple (for learners) and to cope with alternative valid answers. For example, you could have single boxes for denominator and numerator that would accept one or more drag-and-drop objects. In the context of your \( K_c = \frac{a+b}{c} \) example, I'm working from the perspective that A, B , and C are drag-and-drop objects so that learners focus on chemistry rather than, say, TeX/mhchem syntax. Still requires the core algabraic equivalence test but side-steps the complexities of, say, input of \( [H^+] \) and recognition/conversion of \( [H^+] \) to A . Apologies if I'm just stating the blinking obvious with this - but you did ask for any suggestions.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: List comparison problem
ResponsesInList.Text:
Chris will probably be able to think of a clever way to do this using the CAS, but the way I can think of is to use multiple answer tests. Make a PRT like: ~ short for Alg equiv. 
```text
                 x1 ~ ta1 ?
                /         \
               Y           N
              /             \
         x2 ~ ta2 ?      x1 ~ ta2 ?
         /       \       /     \
        Y         N     N       Y
       /           \   /         \
    Right          Wrong      x2 ~ ta1 ?
                              /      \
                             N        Y
                            /          \
                         Wrong        Right
```

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: List comparison problem
ResponsesInList.Text: Harshad, I'll certainly help if I can.  I hate to be picky, but in your example you have given a set of numbers {x1, x2}, rather than a list [x1,x2].  This difference does matter in STACK . Are you using two answer boxes to let the student enter two numbers?  If so, have one PRT where you use the AlgEquiv to test a set you make with {ans1,ans2} with another set made up of the teacher's answers.  Of course, as you say order does matter. I'm guessing that you are asking students to solve a quadratic equation.  Is that correct? The student will provide a list/set of numbers and you need to check if they are correct and complete? Well, in this case to check each element of the student's set/list satisfies the equation I'd suggest that you take each answer and see if it satisfies the equation by substituting in the value. So, if (for argument's sake) you have a random quadratic expression p:2*x^2+11*x-5/4 Then you can ev(p,x=ta1) and check algebraic equivalence with zero. Asking students to solve equations is quite a common thing to want to do.  So, rather than answer here I've add this as an example in STACK's documentation.  See https://github.com/maths/moodle-qtype_stack/blob/master/doc/en/CAS/Equations.md I've also added a new question to the sample questions folder illustrating this. If this is *not* what you wanted to do, please try to describe it in more detail and I'll help. Chris

ResponsesInList.Title: STACK: Customizing the "Int" answer test
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello With STACK questions relating to indefinite integration, the "Int" answer test is typically used (at least in the examples that come with it). The test works fine for us as such, but I wonder whether it's possible (via parameters, assumptions on Maxima variables, or otherwise) to customize its behaviour? For example, I'd like to change it so that: it does not insist on a constant of integration being given, it does not insist on using absolute values inside the argument of logarithms. E.g., if the question reads "find an antiderivative of \( f(x)=1/x \) in the region \( x>0\) ", then \( \log x \) would be a valid answer, not only \( \log \lvert x \rvert + c \) . One solution I can think of is to differentiate the student's answer instead, and compare that to expected results, but in this way I'd probably lose a lot of feedback options that automatically come with the "Int" test.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: STACK: Customizing the "Int" answer test
ResponsesInList.Text: Henning, This is a good point, and I've given some thought to this over the years.  Yes, the constant of integration is currently required.  Adding an option to be strict about this is probably needed.  Colleagues do have very strong views about things like this, but I don't want to be dogmatic. The behaviour of the logarithm case is already defined in the docs (which you have local to your system and which match your version) or online at, e.g. https://github.com/maths/moodle-qtype_stack/blob/master/doc/en/Authoring/Answer_tests.md Have you seen the test script (e.g. http://[YOUR SERVER ]/moodle/question/type/stack/answertests.php?anstest=Int ) which is available to system admins?  The primary purpose of this is to act as unit tests, but exposing the tests also helps users understand how STACK is supposed to (or rather currently) behaves. Below is some of the output from my demo server (a little out of date) for the Int test with logarithms. The answer test responds to *how the teacher* enters their answer. If the teacher uses \( \log(|x|)+c \) in their answer, then they would expect the student to do so. This seemed to be to be a sensible way to pass this option into STACK without creating options (which teachers needs to understand and set correctly!). Can you suggest a mechanism to ignore the constant of integration which is easy for teachers to use?  I think this should be in the list of options to the test perhaps?  If not set the test should degrade gracefully to the existing (strict) behaviour for back compatibility.  Something like passing a list [x, NOCONST] would tell the test not to test for a constant of integration. Currently, if the teacher passes the option as a list to the ATInt then the second argument is taken to be the teacher's answer, used for feedback purposes.  (Not shown below in the examples). We could add to this mechanism. We could have [x, NOCONST=0.5] where the right hand side of the equation is the raw score in the case that the note ATInt_const is generated.  I.e.e the teacher specifies what the score should be in this case. Please send me more test cases!  Please suggest other behaviour (with examples) and I'll see what I can do.  I'm sure this option would be easy to add, and it is a very sensible suggestion (even if I'd never permit my students to ignore the constant of integration!) Chris Sloppy logs (teacher ignores abs(x) ) Pass ln(x) ln(x) x 0 0 You need to add a constant of integration, otherwise this appears to be correct. Well done. ATInt_const. Pass ln(x)+c ln(x)+c x 1 1 ATInt_true. Pass ln(k*x) ln(x)+c x 1 1 ATInt_true. However, your answer differs from the correct answer in a significant way, that is to say not just, e.g., a constant of integration. Please ask your teacher about this. ATInt_EqFormalDiff. Pass ln(abs(x)) ln(abs(x))+c x 0 0 You need to add a constant of integration, otherwise this appears to be correct. Well done. ATInt_const. Pass ln(abs(x))+c ln(abs(x))+c x 1 1 ATInt_true. Pass ln(k*x) ln(abs(x))+c x 0 0 The formal derivative of your answer does equal the expression that you were asked to integrate. However, your answer differs from the correct answer in a significant way, that is to say not just, e.g., a constant of integration. Please ask your teacher about this. ATInt_EqFormalDiff. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: STACK: Customizing the "Int" answer test
ResponsesInList.Text: I have added an additional option to the integration answer test which condones a lack of a constant of integration. On reflection, I have decided not to add the option for partial credit I mentioned above.  Currently, answer tests only return "true" or "false" and partial credit is dealt with at the PRT level.  I'd like to keep the design clean in this respect.  You can now use the ATInt without condoning the lack of a constant in the normal way.  The student gets zero marks and feedback "You need to add a constant of integration".  Then the false branch takes you to another node with the integration answer test with the NOCONST option.  If this returns "true" then you can award whatever partial credit you decide. This code has been committed to the master branch: https://github.com/maths/moodle-qtype_stack/commit/90687b96678065730830aa0447d7e119716dcce4 It will arrive in a tagged release in due course. Comments, examples etc, welcome. Chris

ResponsesInList.Title: Question import plug-in with support for Word and MathType equations
ResponsesInList.Text: I created a Moodle2Word plug-in to support importing and exporting questions to and from Microsoft Word a few years ago. I have now released an update to this plug-in with support for equations which readers of this forum may be interested in. If you use Microsoft Word, and either MathType or the native Microsoft Word Equation Editor to insert equations, you can create and import quiz questions into Moodle question banks. The equations will be converted into images when you upload the questions. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: What is the best option for Mathematics authoring tool and equation editor
ResponsesInList.Text: As Derek suggests, this is a very complex question, it currently has no definitive answer. I have found that even though computers are so heavily wrapped by maths, in every stage of their development and operation, Maths is the one subject they are really poor at in its presentation. Whether it be Arithmetic, Algebra, Calculus or anything else, including representing physics, chemistry, biology or any other form of scientific Maths.  (I am not a dev, and my programming days are long gone, so really cannot explain why this is still the case.) Having said that, the one tool I have found that does work in a normal web environment, and can work in a Moodle is TeX, more specifically TeXLive. There are many different brands of TeX, and a decent TeX filter is not easy to find, but this is the best I have found so far. The syntax is pretty clear, but involved, so there is a learning curve. There is a lot of online, free, manuals available to give anyone who can read a good chance at picking it up relatively quickly though. These forums have TeXLive activated, but the release versions can have support for TeXLive or MathJax relatively easily installed. Solve \( e^{5x} \) for x giving an exact expression. (Using MathJax) When using roots of squares, arguments can become tedious, $$\sqrt{4^2}=4$$ or some logarithms are obvious $$log_{10}100 = 2$$ The two above are TeX. And the presentation here is not what I would like to see in my student's work. That, I think, is Atto, just using an arbitrary centred alignment rather than allowing a user choice the TeX, but it aligns the MathJax properly. An alternative though can be using the Generico filter and importing WolframAlpha widgets for people to use. Whether that can be made available to students, though, without giving them editing capability, I can't say.  That, I suspect, is going to be the sticking point.

ResponsesInList.Title: Help developing a "simple" question using STACK
ResponsesInList.Text: I'm currently running a test for UNSW within the Faculty's of Engineering and Science to see if the STACK plugin meets our needs and if we should proceed to having our Moodle host look into installing it into our production Moodle instance. My first impressions are very positive of this tool and its features, nicely done. During our testing however an academic has come up with a question they'd like to build that I'm having issues with. The question is: A pendulum is located on {["Mercury","Earth","Mars"]} . What length should the pendulum have in order to have a period of {period}s? ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Help developing a "simple" question using STACK
ResponsesInList.Text: It is best to store the word in a variable, so in the Question variables, set planetindex: rand(3)+1 planetname: ["Mercury","Earth","Mars"][planetindex] gravity: [3.61,9.8,3.75][planetindex] Then in the Question text, you can do A pendulum is located on @planetname@. ... Note that, having used rand(), you also need to give the question a Question note, e.g. Pendulum on @planetname@

ResponsesInList.Title: Release of STACK 3.4
ResponsesInList.Text:
Dear all, It gives me great pleasure to announce that we have tagged a new release of STACK :  STACK 3.4. STACK is an optional question type for the Moodle quiz.  This question type uses computer algebra to randomly generate mathematical questions and assess algebraic expressions which students type in as their answers.  A demonstration server is available at http://stack.bham.ac.uk/moodle (Note, this is not running the latest version as I have recently moved to Edinburgh and am in the process of setting up a new demonstration site here.) The changes in this version are all minor improvements, and bug fixes.  There are no substantial changes to features or behaviour which should significantly affect existing users.  We have tagged this release now to enable people relying on managed Moodle environments to obtain the plugin from the catalogue. This has been a very busy and exciting year for the STACK project.  Version 3 is rather well tested now and is increasingly widely used in a variety of languages, teaching situations and in places on a very large scale indeed. As lead developer my focus this year has been on supporting users and teachers, rather than on implementing a raft of new features.  This includes a number of large projects involving collaborations between many universities.  (STACK has also successfully been ported to another VLE: ILIAS.)  I'd like to encourage representatives of those projects to post in this forum, as these experiences will be valuable to others starting out in online assessment. That said, and looking to the future, we have some very exciting and significant changes in the pipeline.  For some of these the code exists in prototype, but for others students are already using them and I'm confident these will be released in the next year. The proposed future changes include the following. (1) Adding "conditional blocks" to the CAS-text environments.  One of the uses of these blocks is to enable the question to "adapt" to the student's answer.  E.g. if a student does not get the answer correct, then the question can adapt to reveal "parts" which the student can type their working.  This profoundly changes the question interaction model available, moving away from a fixed number of answer boxes at the outset.  Blocks are also useful for random versions and embeded images. (2) Adding "reasoning by equivalence" checking.  Here a student works line by line, transforming their equation into a "solved form". An example is shown below . On the left is what the student types into to STACK, and on the right is how the system evaluates this argument. 
```text
x^2-x=30
x^2-x-30=0
(x-6)*(x+5)=0
x-6=0 or x+5=0
x=6 or x=-5
```
 \[\begin{array}{cc} \ & x^2-x=30 & \mbox{ } \\ \color{green}{\Leftrightarrow} & x^2-x-30=0 \\ \color{green}{\Leftrightarrow} & \left(x-6\right)\cdot \left(x+5\right)=0 \\ \color{green}{\Leftrightarrow} & x-6=0\lor x+5=0 \\ \color{green}{\Leftrightarrow} & x=6\lor x=-5 \end{array}\] This is very close to traditional working, and we can now automate the assessment of student's working when presented in this form.  Here, there is no limit on the number of steps, or on which steps a student takes.  Provided adjacent expressions remain "equivalent", the system will accept the argument.  The goal is to rewrite the final answer in a traditional way, e.g. \(x=6 \mbox{ or } x=-5\) .  Some recent research I undertook suggests about 1/3 of the marks available for current International Baccalaureate questions are awarded for precisely this activity. That is to say, reasoning by equivalence is an essential mathematical activity at the hart of elementary pure mathematics, and it forms the basis from which students develop proofs.  Indeed, many proofs such as mathematical induction and \(\epsilon-\delta\) proofs in analysis make use of reasoning by equivalence as part of a wider logical argument. These changes are being developed in parallel and when combined will offer significant benefits to students.  E.g. one use case we envisage is that a student gets an answer wrong, then the blocks will reveal the equivalence input environment where a student can type in their working to help identify any steps with a mistake.  The blocks are being led at Aalto university in Finland, and I am leading the development of reasoning by equivalence. These developments are not secret and I'd very much welcome comments on the design, development, documentation and testing. Of course, other ideas are welcome. If you would like to contribute, please contact me.  Please don't overestimate the level of knowledge needed to contribute.  Proof reading the documentation, and editing this as a new user with "things I wish I'd known" is an immensely valuable contribution to the project!  Please contribute sample questions, experiences and evaluations of use with students. I'd like to thank Tim Hunt at the OU for his continued support and advice, particularly on the quiz aspects and Matti Harjula at Aalto, Finland, for his ongoing work on developing STACK. Chris Sangwin

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: MathJAX notation not appearing in matching question answers
ResponsesInList.Text:
MathJax is not actually part of Moodle, but is a separate javascript library from mathjax.org. The MathJax filter loads the library from a url specified in the settings. If you have an older version of Moodle, you can change this setting to http://cdn.mathjax.org/mathjax/2.5-latest/MathJax.js to switch versions. There is also a configuration setting that configures MathJax defaults.  The user can normally set the display mode by right clicking any mathematical expression and finding the desired option. (You should try this to test your question first). The default renderer can be specified with the MathJax configuration in the settings, by adding something like 
```text
MMLorHTML
:
 
{

    
prefer
:
 
{

      Chrome
:
 
"CommonHTML"

    
}

  
}
```
 See the MathJax Documentation . This may work, but no guarantee. You will need to test it. Installing a different question type, may be easier.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: MathJAX notation not appearing in matching question answers
ResponsesInList.Text: Daniel, the point here is that no matter what settings of MathJax or other math renderers are selected you can't change the behaviour of browsers using <option> tags. Permitted content is only Text with eventually escaped characters (like é). You can use html entities and unicode characters there but no html elements inside option tag. The only browser that can render some html inside <option> tags is Firefox but it's not valid html (in this case Firefox breaks the rules - not IE or Chrome) - see https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/option If the dropdown lists in quizzes were built for example with <li> tags dropdown lists could use flow content like modern navigation menus nowadays do. It would allow all kinds of selection lists with all kinds of answer options.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: MathJAX notation not appearing in matching question answers
ResponsesInList.Text: There is no cross-browser way to style select and option elements and therefore only FF (Mozilla) browsers render any maths in drop down lists in Quiz. The best workaround would be to replace those traditional dropdown lists (select and option html tags) with pure css based or javascript based "drop down lists" that use other elements - for example normal ul & li elements like navigation blocks and this way drop down lists could use any math renderer and show images in those lists as well. For example Bootstrap themes have built in css classes for such lists called Button dropdowns.

ResponsesInList.Title: STACK: display format
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi, Probably it is a easy, but ... It is a simple calculation (2 + sqrt (2)) * sqrt (2) and STACK returns the result as 2 ^ (3/2) +2 but I need 2sqrt (2) + 2 . What am I doing wrong?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: STACK: display format
ResponsesInList.Text: Jerry, Thanks for posting this. STACK uses the Maxima variable "sqrtdispflag" to control the display of fractional powers with the surd symbol or fractional powers.  However, internally, STACK uses only fractional powers. For example, start a Maxima desktop and type in sqrt(2). p:sqrt(2); Then use this command to inspect the internal representation: ?print(p); The result is ((MEXPT SIMP) 2 ((RAT SIMP) 1 2)) So, internally the sqrt has been turned into a fractional power.  CAS don't like having two different internal representations for the same thing.  Maxima's display routines look at the "sqrtdispflag" and turn some back into surds. What you've asked for is actually one of the more difficult things to achieve, because really we are trying to be inconsistent here!  When we distribute the product as step 1 we have (2 + sqrt (2)) * sqrt (2) -> 2 * sqrt (2) + sqrt (2) * sqrt (2 ) Then we sort out the powers.  This is the problem.  If we transform products of powers of 2 into a single power of 2 the second one becomes 2^1=2, the first one also becomes 2^(3/2) which is what you see. I'm not sure what to suggest.  What you've asked for is a very sensible request. I'll give some thought to how we can achieve it (I'm sure it must be possible.....) Chris

ResponsesInList.Title: STACK 3.0 Beta
ResponsesInList.Text: It gives me great pleasure to announce the release of STACK 3.0 beta. In Jan 2012 we decided to move STACK development in a new direction to develop a question type for the Moodle quiz. Since then we have made steady and significant progress. We are now ready to release beta code for testing and further development. The code is available at https://github.com/maths/moodle-qtype_stack/ All the key components are in place, but not all the features have been re-implemented. In particular, we have not re-implemented some of the input mechanisms. If these are important to you then please let me know. I am very grateful to Phil Butcher of the OU for his support. Tim Hunt has also been a key collaborator, writing question behaviours for STACK and writing substantial portions of the code closest to Moodle itself. This joint work has enabled usto make some important minor changes to the Moodle core which are key to the integration of STACK fully. I would also like to thank (1) Matti Pauna for working on the qformat_stack code which imports STACK 2 questions into STACK 3, (2) Matti Harjula for the server which increases the efficiency of the connection to Maxima, and (3) to Mikael Kurula for testing and the contribution of a Swedish translation. STACK is an open source and collaborative project. There is still substantial work to make sure it is a useful and reliable tool. I would very much welcome further collaborations, in testing, translations and in further adding back the remaining features. Help by with the documentation would also be most welcome, particularly with (a) step-by-step guides and (b) I wish I had known "...." information. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: STACK 3.0 Beta
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Ben! Very nice that you're interested in STACK! To try to answer a few of your questions: 1. Deployment is connected to randomized questions. If you author a question with random parameters, then the solution of the problem might depend on the values of the parameters in an undesired way. The students get randomly chosen instances among those that you have deployed. Questions not using randomization don't need to be deployed. 2. The question note is also used with random questions. STACK uses the question note to distinguish between two random instances of the same question, e.g. when deploying. And this is also useful for reviewing after your course is done. The question note should include all random variables. Personally, I would write something like "Derivative of @expression@ is @diff(expression,x)@", if expression is a random function of x that should be differentiated. I don't know if that is good or bad, but that's how I started doing it. I'm not sure it's a good idea to make entering the question note automatically, since it might not be easy to read later, when you review. 3. You can already now plot things, with or without randomization, using the plot command. 4. The point of the automated question tests is to automatically test the functionality of your question, and try to make sure that you don't accidentally break something by editing your question. Therefore you should add at least one test case for every possible way of traversing the potential response trees (PRTs), in order to make sure that the outcome is the correct one for a given input. I don't see how you can replace this by adding cases to the PRTs, because the question tests are precisely supposed to verify that these PRT cases work properly. Indeed, you should try to predict what mistakes a student could make and add tests that capture these in the PRTs. Here the answer note is again useful for reviewing. 5. A screen cast would be very good! Please post the link if you create something! These Authoring quick start questions should get you up and running very quickly. 6. I didn't understand your comments on CAS text. If I'm not mistaken, then the CAS text is precisely what goes between the @ signs. See here . In the CAS Chat, you need to enclose whatever you want Maxima to evaluate between @ signs, IIRC. In your case, type in @3-1;@ and see what happens. 7. About the input and answer tests I don't know, that's a question for Chris and Tim, I guess. Hope this can be of some help, Mikael

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Strange Feedback by "Int" in STACK
ResponsesInList.Text: Mikko, The answer test only has the *teacher's answer*.  To provide this feedback, the system has to infer what the teacher has set in the question.  This includes stripping off constants of integration.  Constants of integration may occur in a number of ways, e.g. \[ \int \frac{1}{x}\mathrm{d}x = \ln(kx).\] I agree the feedback looks very odd.  I think this code needs to be re-factored, but I'm not sure how.  I've added an issue so I don't loose this suggestion. https://github.com/maths/moodle-qtype_stack/issues/126 When this happens, use the "Quiet" option and provide bespoke feedback for this question.  I'm sorry this happens in a demo question....

If MathJax does not have some symbols that old latex distribution (Tex filter) had you can use macros or unicode symbols. For example you could try to add to MathJax configuration inside TeX: { ... } (after extensions) TeX: {
                    extensions: ["mhchem.js"],
          Macros: {
            /* Wikipedia compatibility: these macros are used on Wikipedia */
            empty: '\\emptyset',
            P: '\\unicode{xb6}', Alpha: '\\unicode{x391}', /* FIXME: These capital Greeks don't show up in bold in \boldsymbol ... */ Beta: '\\unicode{x392}', Epsilon: '\\unicode{x395}', Zeta: '\\unicode{x396}', Eta: '\\unicode{x397}', Iota: '\\unicode{x399}', Kappa: '\\unicode{x39a}', Mu: '\\unicode{x39c}', Nu: '\\unicode{x39d}', Just remember to use backslash when you type those new macros like \Z. If you need some special character that does not have latex symbol you can use in mathjax \unicode{...} - for example \unicode{8484} creates \( \unicode{8484} \) - or you can even copy and paste (or write) normal unicode characters inside mathjax delimiters to mathematical notations (the number is useful only if you can't find or type an unicode character otherwise)

ResponsesInList.Title: Embedding Mathslate editor in questions with filter
ResponsesInList.Text: After the discussion of embedding Desmos in quiz questions, I decided to try to create a filter to embed the Mathslate mathematics editor into quiz questions.  I have a reasonably good for version available now .  Before installing you will need to upgrade the TinyMCE Mathslate to the latest version in my github . Then make sure that MathJax and the TinyMCE version are working correctly. The filter is used to insert a drag and drop editor instance in front of a text input box.  It should work with short answer, embedded, essay, formula, algebra, and STACK question types.  While editing a question's text inserting {MATHSLATE:type=default,format=tex} will insert a standard Mathslate editor in front of the next input element that appears in HTML of the question.  The expression in Mathslate work area will be copied to the input element to be checked when the question or quiz is submitted. Different configurations of the editor can be specified with the type parameter above.  Each type is specified by a JSON configuration file.  If this file supports more output formats these can be specified with the format parameter.

ResponsesInList.Title: Tex filter or MathJax filter?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi! I'm not able to find significant reasons why choose MathJax filter instead of the core Tex notation filter to render tex expressions. I'm sure I may be missing something... Can anyone please give me some reasons? Thank you! Best regards, susana

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Tex filter or MathJax filter?
ResponsesInList.Text: Good question Susana, and for me, it is only a personal choice. I have become a little familiar with TeX over the years and I actually find it easier to just code things, but having said that, for anyone not familiar with TeX, or coding standards, building expressions and equations using MathJax is a lot less of a learning curve. I found that a lot of other Maths and Science teachers want easy, less time consuming tools to do things, so have them using MathJax rather than try and teach them TeX. Saves me a lot of argument, ego wrestling and dummy spitting.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Tex filter or MathJax filter?
ResponsesInList.Text: For typical user it does not matter (a lot) which filter you select - if you need to use a filter - both filters allow some features of (La)TeX and restrict many advanced features of Latex and MathJax. In both filters you have options to change many default settings in administration menu so you can also enable Tex filter and use MathJax with any configuration (and custom delimiters) through Additional HTML (Site administration > Appearance > Additional HTML). Some advantages of MathJax are reported in http://www.mathjax.org/ and you can also check pages like http://www.math.union.edu/~dpvc/talks/2013-01-11.jmm/TOC.html - note however that default settings of MathJax filter do not use all the features of those small demos. For example you can use colors in syntax: \[ \bbox[#FD9,border:2px solid purple,10px]{ \bbox[red]{r} + \bbox[green,5px]{\color{yellow}{g}} + \bbox[border:2px dashed blue,3px]{b} } \] Typically MathJax takes font color from surrounding text (HTML elements) $$ x = {-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}\over 2a} $$ so you can use normal html tags to style or scale mathematical elements or even unicode characters with styles $$ \unicode{10086} $$

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Tex filter or MathJax filter?
ResponsesInList.Text: As detailed in a parallel thread , with Moodle 2.8 it is now possible to have both the MathJax and TeX filters enabled. All other things being equal, I prefer MathJax for better accessibility and better quality of rendering (though the new SVG TeX rendering, in Moodle 2.8 is also good). Also, it is relatively easy to add MathJax support to other Moodle-linked e-Learning applications such as Mahara . So, you can give your users a reasonably consistent experience in rendering equations etc on different systems. Since Google Chrome/Chromium dropped support for MathML, MathJax has become the de facto standard for Maths display on the Web. That said, for complex content MathJax rendering can be slow. Having (cached) SVG/PNG TeX rendering as well can help with this. Also, the recently released MathJax 2.5 is reported to have significant performance improvements. On occasion, you may encounter MathJax clashes with other JavaScript / AJAX libraries, e.g. perhaps with some third-party Moodle modules. In such cases just using the TeX filter alone may provide a useful workaround.
